title: Shepherd's pie
description: Pie of minced meat topped with mashed potato
wiki_lead:
Shepherd's pie, cottage pie, or in French cuisine hachis Parmentier, is a savoury dish of cooked minced meat topped with mashed potato and baked, formerly also called Sanders or Saunders. The meat used may be either previously cooked or freshly minced. The terms shepherd's pie and cottage pie have been used interchangeably since they came into use in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, although some writers insist that a shepherd's pie should contain lamb or mutton, and a cottage pie, beef.
The term "cottage pie" is first recorded in 1791. "Shepherd's pie" is later, first recorded in the nineteenth century. Some modern variations are vegetarian or vegan, using substitutes for meat and dairy ingredients.

Shepherd's pie, cottage pie, or in French cuisine hachis Parmentier, is a savoury dish of cooked minced meat topped with mashed potato and baked, formerly also called Sanders or Saunders. The meat used may be either previously cooked or freshly minced. The terms shepherd's pie and cottage pie have been used interchangeably since they came into use in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, although some writers insist that a shepherd's pie should contain lamb or mutton, and a cottage pie, beef.
The term "cottage pie" is first recorded in 1791. "Shepherd's pie" is later, first recorded in the nineteenth century. Some modern variations are vegetarian or vegan, using substitutes for meat and dairy ingredients.


Definitions and preparation
Some people in Britain call the pies made with beef "cottage pies" and those with lamb, "shepherd's pies". The major supermarkets do so, and the distinction is backed by some reference works. Other authorities and cooks and food writers including Prue Leith, Caroline Waldegrave and John Ayto regard the two names as completely interchangeable. Jane Grigson's 1974 recipe for shepherd's pie uses beef, and mentions that it is "sometimes called" cottage pie.
In Australia, Canada, and the US, "shepherd's pie" is a common term for a dish of any meat covered in mashed potato. Food retailers in those countries apply the term "shepherd's pie" to beef-filled pies as well as those containing lamb.
A basic shepherd's pie consists of cooked minced meat covered with mashed potatoes. It is baked.


History


Cottage pie
The term was in use by 1791. Parson Woodforde mentions "Cottage-Pye" in his diary entry for 29 August 1791 and several times thereafter. He records that the meat was veal but does not say what the topping was. The dish was known under a different name in the early 19th century: in 1806, in her book A New System of Domestic Cookery, Maria Rundell published a recipe for "Sanders", consisting of minced beef or mutton, with onion and gravy, topped with mashed potato and baked as individual servings. Sanders or Saunders could also have a filling of sliced meat. According to Jane Grigson in English Food, mincing originally meant chopping something with a knife. "But with the first mincing-machines, prison, school and seaside boarding house cooks acquired a new weapon to depress their victims, with watery mince, shepherd's pie with rubbery granules of left-over meat."
In 20th-century and later British usage the term cottage pie has widely, but not exclusively, been used for a dish of chopped or minced beef with a mashed potato topping. Grigson records that that to make the dish go further, some recipes put in a bottom layer of potato before adding the meat and top layer. The meat may be raw or previously cooked; the latter was at one time more usual. grok_lead: Shepherd's pie is a traditional savory casserole originating from the United Kingdom and Ireland, consisting of cooked minced lamb mixed with vegetables and gravy, topped with a layer of mashed potatoes and baked until golden. The dish is distinguished from the similar cottage pie by its use of lamb or mutton as the primary meat, reflecting its pastoral associations, while cottage pie traditionally employs ground beef. The origins of shepherd's pie trace back to the late 18th century, evolving as a frugal meal for rural laborers and cottagers who repurposed leftover roasted meat and potatoes, a staple introduced to the British Isles in the late 16th century by explorers like Sir Walter Raleigh. The term "cottage pie" first appeared in print in 1791 in the diary of Reverend James Woodforde, describing a simple potato-topped meat dish, while "shepherd's pie" emerged around 1849 in Scottish records and gained wider use by the mid-19th century to specify the lamb version. This evolution coincided with socio-economic hardships, including the Great Famine in Ireland, where the dish symbolized resourcefulness among shepherds and peasants. Both Britain and Ireland claim the dish, though the lamb-based preparation is more closely tied to Irish culinary traditions. Key ingredients typically include ground lamb, onions, carrots, celery, and peas simmered in a gravy flavored with Worcestershire sauce, tomato paste, and herbs like thyme and rosemary, all covered by creamy mashed potatoes often enriched with butter and milk. Variations may incorporate beef stock for depth or additional seasonings, but the core remains a one-dish comfort food baked to meld flavors. Over time, the recipe has spread globally, inspiring adaptations like the French hachis parmentier, while retaining its status as a hearty emblem of British Isles home cooking.
